title: Network Delay Time
statement:
A network has `n` nodes labelled `1` to `n`. Each entry `times[i] = [u, v, w]` is a **directed** link: a signal sent from `u` reaches `v` after `w` time units.

A signal is sent from node `k` at time 0 and spreads along every link. Return how long it takes until **every** node has received it, or `-1` if some node can never be reached.

No `(u, v)` pair appears twice, and there are no self-loops.

target.note: Dijkstra with a binary heap is O(E log E); the bench has n edges over n/4 nodes

hints: The time a node receives the signal is the length of the shortest weighted path from k to it, and the answer is the largest of those. Why doesn't plain BFS find those shortest paths here?

With non-negative weights, Dijkstra's algorithm works: always settle the unsettled node with the smallest tentative distance, because no later path can beat it. A min-heap gives you that node quickly.

Build adjacency lists. dist[] starts at infinity, with dist[k] = 0. Push (k, 0) onto a PriorityQueue ordered by distance. Pop; if the popped distance is larger than dist[node], skip it (it's stale); otherwise relax each outgoing edge, pushing (v, newDist) when it improves. At the end, return -1 if any dist is still infinity, else the max.
followups: Why does Dijkstra break with negative weights, and what would you use instead?
This uses lazy deletion (stale heap entries are skipped). What is a decrease-key, and why doesn't Java's PriorityQueue offer one?
With n ≤ 100 and a dense graph, would the O(V^2) array version of Dijkstra be faster? Why?
explain: Each node receives the signal at the time of its shortest weighted path from k, so run single-source shortest paths and take the maximum. If any node is unreachable, return -1. Weights are non-negative, so use Dijkstra. Keep a PriorityQueue of (node, distance). When a node is popped with its current best distance, that distance is final, because every other route costs at least as much. Relax its out-edges and push any improvement. Java's PriorityQueue has no decrease-key, so you push duplicates and skip stale entries whose popped distance exceeds dist[node]. That's O(E log E) = O(E log V) time and O(V + E) space. Order the heap with Integer.compare, and don't add to an infinite distance: only relax from nodes that were actually popped. BFS is wrong here because the fewest hops isn't the least time. Bellman-Ford's O(V·E) handles negative weights but is far slower.
